body.text: Three hours into last Friday’s hearing of the parliamentary inquiry examining artificial intelligence, Nationals senator Ross Cadell asked a straightforward question about copyright. The answer he received may say more about why Silicon Valley frontier AI companies want Australia’s law changed than anything they have said themselves.

Cadell asked officials from the Attorney-General’s Department whether, if the companies brought their operations to Australia, they would be training new AI models solely on Australian creative material. “Or is it all material globally that we’re worried about them using if they come to Australia?” The officials said it was both.

“Copyright works on a territorial basis,” assistant secretary Jenna Priestly explained. “It’s the country in which the activity occurs whose law applies, rather than the origin of the material itself. So Australia’s Copyright Act protects material that’s Australian in origin but also creative material from across the world.”
Cadell asked if that meant Australia’s standards would apply to all material AI companies fed into their models during training in Australia, regardless of where it was created.
“That’s right,” Priestly said.

It confirmed the senator’s suspicions. Copyright law worldwide, governed by the Berne Convention, is based on a common principle that creators have automatic rights over their content and are entitled to control how it is used. The tacit flipside to Priestly’s explanation was that changing what governs such protection in Australia could potentially weaken protection for rights-holders globally whose works are copied in Australia.
The Nationals senator triple-checked his understanding.
“So, it’s not just Australian stuff that they want access to — it’s around the world, with our laws?”
There was a moment of silence. The officials nodded but didn’t speak.
“Right,” Cadell said.

AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI are leaning hard on the federal government to modify copyright laws so they can move training of future models to Australia to access rights-holders’ work without having to negotiate licences. The companies are not willing to strike agreements to pay for permission to scrape Australian books, blogs, journalism, music and lyrics, screen productions, visual art, gaming code, and other data to train new and more capable AI models. The government has ruled out a complete text and data-mining exemption for AI but not other potential modifications to blanket protections. The one-and-done alternative compensation system the companies want would provide them with a highly advantageous, hidden loophole.
Opponents of the proposed changes say they would actually affect rights-holders everywhere and risk making Australia an international copyright pariah.

The companies want a decision urgently, insisting they will go elsewhere if it doesn’t come soon. Alternative locations have been mentioned: Japan, Singapore, Canada and Britain. But Britain has ruled out copyright changes, Canada has complicated laws and is brawling with the US, Singapore isn’t far from China and although Japan has a text-and-data-mining exemption, it’s not clearcut. Staying in the US, with its unpredictable president, is now their alternative.
Any change to Australia’s copyright law will need legislation, raising the prospect of difficult negotiations in the Senate either with the opposition or with the Greens and crossbench.

Senator Ross Cadell doesn’t buy the all-or-nothing threats. “They have a significant preference for us, I would say,” he says of the companies, “so I don’t think we should give them everything they’re after.”
Another committee member, independent ACT senator David Pocock, received leaked details recently of a proposed option featuring in negotiations. Pocock questions the urgency and the need.

“I would have thought in the first instance, you’d say ‘We’ve got a copyright system here, we’ve got a free market, you need to go and negotiate’,” Pocock tells Inside Story. “And if that doesn’t work, then sure, maybe parliament needs to look at other ways around. And, you know, I think we still do have time. None of these Anthropic or OpenAI data centres are going to build themselves in the next six months or twelve months. So, let’s actually get this right.”

Underpinning the Australian copyright standoff on display during the week’s committee hearings is an expectation that AI will rapidly divide the world into nations where frontier models are developed — currently only the US and China — and the rest, and that the rest will also cleave. The government believes Australia can either become indispensable to the technology’s developers or relegated to just being a customer. Its strong view is that becoming an alternate training site for US labs is the only way a non-frontier country can embed itself in the AI revolution and insulate its citizens from the monumental economic upheaval and security threats the same technology will bring. Without that advantage, they fear the tech onslaught could hollow out the economy and leave systems unprotected from powerful models capable of attack.
The American companies also argue they must be supported to outrun Chinese competitors for global security reasons. Pocock asks how watering down the law in a democracy is the answer to that.

“I think it probably strengthens the argument to actually work through diplomatic channels and create some sort of country-to-country agreements on the pace of the frontier, access to frontier models, the direction all this is heading in,” he says. “Instead, we’re doing basically exactly what these tech bros seem to want and negotiating with them like they’re sovereign nations.”

The frontier companies’ public reasoning for favouring Australia as a new training hub dwells on open space, water, energy opportunities and a stable democratic political system — all significant attributes when AI training and processing require massive data centres and consistent access to resources. While Australians’ pushback against data centres appears to be growing, it has not reached the scale of the backlash in America, where some states have introduced moratoriums. Here, the social licence is fragile but, the government hopes, still valid.

There are good reasons for the frontier labs to come here and good reasons to encourage them. But the companies object to being required to strike licence agreements for access to creative works. AI models learn by ingesting many forms of human language and the developers insist the volume of material required to keep increasing their potentially world-changing capabilities makes doing deals, sector by sector, with rights bodies unworkable.

What the companies haven’t said out loud is now becoming clear: having the government modify Australian copyright law could make it much harder for creatives in the rest of the world to protect their work from being scraped. Copyright specialist and partner with Marque Lawyers Emma Johnsen says it’s a live issue.

“Copyright is territorial but AI companies can choose the territory,” Johnsen tells Inside Story. “So, if Australia makes commercial AI training materially easier, then companies may have an incentive to move their copying here. And that could affect not just Australian creators but copyright owners all around the world, because they [the companies] know that their works could be copied legally in Australia. We would potentially become the safe haven for copying.”
The companies call copyright their red line: they won’t move their training to Australia, with all the economic, technological and security benefits that would bring, unless the law is changed.

In lieu of separate agreements, the proposed copyright overhaul would involve the companies paying into a central fund in Australia to compensate Australian creators willing to have their work used for AI-model training. The government would manage the fund and payment distribution. Those unwilling to participate would need to register to opt out, putting a digital marker on what was out of bounds and trusting this, and the labs, to isolate it. Doing neither, or not realising you need to, would render the work fair game.
Pocock has some fundamental concerns with potentially forfeiting a system that recognises human creativity to make way for artificial intelligence.

“At a human level, what we’re actually talking about is essentially selling out humans and their work for machines to replace human work,” Pocock tells Inside Story. “That’s really what it is we’re saying. All these things that humans have created — we’ve built a copyright system because we have recognised that this belongs to them, this is created by them — we’re essentially, potentially going to say, ‘Well, yeah, that doesn’t matter because machines will be able to do it better and that’s really important’.”

Missing, even from the fine print, is the proposal’s other catch. Rights-holders everywhere else — all around the world — would also need to register their works for opt-out protection in Australia, requiring every creator worldwide to know about, and act on, the requirement. Otherwise, they would potentially give the frontier companies free access provided the copying is done here. The opt-in fund wouldn’t cover international works so those authors, composers and filmmakers would receive no payment.

The government argues that changing the law could give Australian rights-holders payment for AI use of their work where now they get none. That is also the companies’ argument. Some in the arts community are deeply uncomfortable at being offered a change that could benefit some Australian creatives at the expense of others, including colleagues around the world — an enticement with echoes of Judas and the thirty pieces of silver.

Nationals senator Ross Cadell also objects to what he believes is the deliberate omission of any reference to the global implications. He says all of the government’s submissions to the parliamentary inquiry refer only to Australian rights-holders.
“What we’re seeing is a proposal that would open the door for every piece of data in the world,” Cadell says. “What it means is a race to the bottom on protections.”

He has “some sympathy” for the companies’ protest at the number of licencing deals that would be required. But he is also cynical about the urgency, suggesting advocacy for data and code rights-holders is not well organised and sealing a deal before that changes might explain the hurry.
Emma Johnsen says an opt-out change could see Australia supplant the US as the companies’ favoured legal jurisdiction.

“At the moment it appears to be America is the safe haven for copying because of the way their fair use laws have been interpreted and are being interpreted,” Johnsen says. “I do think there is a real risk that Australia could become a weak link if we make our copyright laws materially more permissive than comparable countries.”

She says the change, if adopted, could have a lowest-common-denominator effect. “It does create a real risk of regulatory arbitrage because companies choose to do the legally significant copying in whichever country gives them the most favourable rules,” she says.

American AI development companies currently do their copying in the US, relying on the local law’s relatively generous “fair use” exemption to justify scraping creative works without paying. Facing more than 140 American law suits, their defence rests heavily on the argument that no licencing market exists for AI use of copyrighted works anywhere — something the Australian creative industries strongly dispute. Although Australia’s copyright licencing system is mostly voluntary, education, government and music broadcasting are subject to compulsory statutory licencing. The affected industries would like to negotiate with the giant frontier labs but say the labs have refused to even try.

Music industry peak bodies the Australian Recording Industry Association and the Phonographic Performance Company of Australia argue in their submission to the AI inquiry that a functioning commercial market exists and the proposed legal change is unjustified. “Commercial inconvenience, a desire to reduce costs, or dissatisfaction with market terms is not evidence of market failure,” they say.
The companies have told the government they need the law changed to help them win those American cases. They haven’t made that argument publicly but some of their advocates are beginning to do so.

Washington-based Australian expatriate AI expert and former Prime Minister’s Department official Janet Egan is backing the labs’ copyright demand. Last month, in an interview with podcaster Joe Walker, she spelled it out. “AI companies won’t pay for a copyright licence in Australia because it will undermine their cases for fair use applicability in the US,” she said, describing what Australia could offer as “a safe harbour.”

Egan said changing copyright law would give Australia leverage to make early-access and other demands of the labs. This is also the government’s argument for having AI-model training onshore. “You can create the conditions to welcome training to Australia, and then because of the first -mover advantage, because companies want to have a guaranteed place to build out their compute, you can ask for a lot in return,” she told the podcast.

The companies say signing licence agreements in Australia would be an effective admission that a licencing market exists, so they need a change in law to deal with the issue another way. In other words, they want Australia to help get around the law in the US which could save them the large sums they’ll owe if they lose the cases and limit their future exposure to litigation.
Emma Johnsen has a different take on how the proposed opt-out provision in Australia would affect a licencing market.

“I think it will affect rights-holders overseas because it could destroy a licencing market before creators from all over the world have had the opportunity to develop it,” she says. “A UK publisher may not be able to have a say in how their works are accessed in Australia, and on what terms, because the government will likely be deciding it for them — which is unusual because right now, copyright holders have the right to engage in those negotiations and decide what the economic value is of the works.”

Johnsen says an Australian opt-out change could undermine the Berne Convention’s declaration that rights are automatic and must not be subject to any “formality,” meaning any administrative requirement or procedural condition, including registration. It could also run foul of the TRIPS Agreement which carries copyright standards into the world trade system.

The Berne Convention sets a three-step test for exceptions from copyright law: they must be special cases which don’t conflict with “a normal exploitation of the work” and don’t unreasonably prejudice “the legitimate interests of the author.” As Johnsen says, “You can have exceptions to copyright but they can’t go too far.”

The Australia–UK Free Trade Agreement allows for copyright exceptions, including for digital and sometimes commercial use, but similarly features the three-step test. Johnsen suggests an opt-out change to Australian law could create “a valid tension” in the FTA.

The Copyright Council is also concerned. It believes a broad exception for text-and-data mining for AI would fail all three parts of the test. In its submission to the parliamentary inquiry, it rejects any suggestion Australian copyright law should change to align with the law elsewhere.

“The push by AI developers for Australia’s copyright law framework to be weakened is not a call for Australia to follow copyright arrangements in other countries but rather for Australia to become a ‘template’ for weaker protection of copyright material worldwide,” its submission says.

The companies have made their own submissions to the inquiry, which will help inform the government’s thinking. OpenAI’s was lodged before the public learned this week that agents — autonomous AI computer programs — from one of its unreleased models had infiltrated an Australian Medicare data website in June. Its submission does not mention the incident but urges Australia to foster international cooperation on AI safety, including “secure channels for sharing findings on advanced capabilities.”
On copyright, it says Australia has the opportunity to create “a clear and durable framework that both respects creators and provides legal certainty for AI development.”

Inside government and among some of the companies’ advocates, meanwhile, the Medicare hack is being seen as a public relations disaster for their copyright campaign. Although it seems only public data was accessed, the incident was believed initially to be the first worldwide to involve AI agents-in-training hacking a government website and made global headlines. On Saturday morning, the New York Times revealed another incidence of rogue, autonomous non-human OpenAI agents entering government sites, this time in the US. It said the company had confirmed its AI agents had “meddled” with websites for the education and commerce departments and the Securities and Exchange Commission, over the northern summer and without the lab’s knowledge. OpenAI was reported as saying it was not a “breach” but that the agents had interacted with the sites in “unusual ways.” The company had notified the US agencies “in recent weeks”, raising new questions about the timing of Albanese’s announcement and whether the governments may have coordinated to flush the company out.
Albanese and other senior ministers are understood to be enraged at OpenAI over the Australian breach, both that it occurred at all and at how the company handled it.

It took three months for OpenAI to notify government and then only Services Australia via a public email inbox. Inside Story has been told ministers and officials have had many conversations with OpenAI representatives about training compute and copyright in the months since the incident occurred, and they never mentioned it.

In New York for the United Nations General Assembly, Albanese conveyed his displeasure to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, who was also in town. The prime minister ordered a rapid review to determine if Australian law needs updating to clarify who is accountable if an AI agent — not a legal person — acts unlawfully. The company is reviewing its procedures.

Albanese rejected opposition suggestions he delayed disclosing the incident so it would coincide with Altman addressing the Security Council. But he and others are known to have been furious that an OpenAI executive gave an interview recently to the Australian turning the labs’ private demands on copyright law into an aggressive public ultimatum.
After this week’s incident, the government is issuing some in return.

“One of the reporting requirements that we expect going forward is that the nature of the disclosure is consistent with the seriousness of the incident and that means it being reported at a senior level and with full information,” assistant minister Andrew Charlton told ABC Radio National on Friday.

The companies are still pushing on copyright, spruiking their eye-watering investments in Australia. Anthropic is urging Australia to help drive “a race to the top on safety, where AI companies compete on safety and safeguards rather than cutting corners.” In its AI inquiry submission, it also calls for legal certainty through “a targeted approval” to train models on copyrighted material involving digital do-not-crawl signals.

“We understand that the government may choose to require investment or other conditions designed to support the future of Australian creators and cultural endeavours,” it says, “and we are open to considering those conditions.”

Some advocates for bringing the companies’ training compute to Australia argue privately that the national economic and security gains in facilitating it — and serious potential prosperity and safety risks in missing out — outweigh creatives’ rights.

Thus far, arts industry representatives are choosing not to speak out against the mooted changes, preferring to make their case behind closed doors. But some close to the discussions say they fear the government’s determination to secure training deals will ultimately be at their expense, and their global colleagues’.
In a July speech setting his course on AI policy, Albanese offered the creative industries what was billed as reassurance.

“Australian writers, musicians, artists and journalists must retain ownership and control of their work,” Albanese said. “Our laws will spell that out, plain as day. An artist’s creative endeavour is their work and their property. No company should use Australian books, music, art or news to build or train AI without the artist’s control. That includes the artist’s control of the price and value of their work. Anything less, is theft.”

He didn’t promise to ensure fair payment, only “ownership” and “control.” Those in the creative industries who knew of the opt-out proposal observed that “control” didn’t rule it out. They noted that a government inclined to accede to the companies by requiring creators to actively include or exclude their own work might choose to justify it that way.

The discussions with industry and the companies are ongoing. Attorney-general Michelle Rowland has carriage of the issue and now is referring to fair recompense. Her spokesperson declined to comment on the implications of the opt-out proposal for rights-holders worldwide, saying: “The government is continuing to consult with creators, media organisations and AI companies on a range of options to ensure any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation.”

In his Friday morning speech to the UN, Albanese pitched for Australia to win a temporary seat on the Security Council, declaring a commitment to uphold international law. “We listen with respect, we partner as equals, and we protect what matters most,” he said. “…We champion the rights, sovereignty and agency of all.” AI, he said, must be subject to standards to ensure it “will work and deliver for people – not the other way around.”

His government is highly sensitive to public anxiety at home about the rise of AI, which hacking incidents only exacerbate. This, and the increasing reports of uncontrolled AI agents entering government and other websites, is not increasing its warmth towards the frontier labs and their chiefs. Inside Story understands Albanese and his ministers are also losing patience with how the companies and its cheerleaders are conveying the copyright demands. They are starting to draw their own red lines. •
